Family Health

Do vitamins help vaginal dryness?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

There is no single best vitamin for vaginal dryness. Some small studies have investigated vitamins and other products, but their results do not make an oral supplement a reliable substitute for assessment and established treatment. The cause of the dryness and the way a product is used both matter.

Dryness is not always a nutritional problem

Lower oestrogen around menopause can affect vaginal and urinary tissues. Dryness can also occur during breastfeeding, with certain medicines or after cancer treatment. Irritating products, skin conditions and other problems may cause overlapping symptoms.

A diet change cannot be assumed to correct all of these causes. Persistent soreness, pain during sex, unusual discharge or urinary symptoms deserve a conversation with a clinician. Tell them about breastfeeding, contraception, medicines and any cancer history.

Do not assume that spotting is simply caused by dryness. Bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause should be checked. Severe pelvic pain, fever or significant bleeding needs more urgent assessment.

Vitamin E and vitamin D: promising results are not a prescription

Small trials of vaginal vitamin E or vitamin D preparations have reported improvements in some symptoms or measures of vaginal tissue health. These studies generally used a particular formulation for a limited time in selected groups.

They do not show that swallowing an ordinary vitamin capsule has the same effect. In an 80-participant trial of oral vitamin D, the treatment group did not improve significantly more than the placebo group on the measured vaginal outcomes. A change within one group alone does not establish a treatment benefit.

Treating a confirmed deficiency or taking an appropriate supplement for bone health may still be worthwhile. That is a separate decision from using vitamins as treatment for vaginal dryness. Do not insert oral capsules or cosmetic vitamin oils into the vagina.

Vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant, while vitamin D has an established role in bone health. Those general roles do not establish a dryness treatment. Some studies combined vitamins E, A or D with other ingredients, so their findings cannot isolate which component helped. An association between blood vitamin D and tissue moisture likewise does not show that raising the level treats symptoms.

Hyaluronic acid: the formulation matters

Hyaluronic acid is used in some vaginal moisturisers. It is not a vitamin, and evidence about a product applied inside the vagina cannot be transferred to a swallowed supplement or a facial serum.

A small trial involving 42 postmenopausal participants tested vaginal hyaluronic-acid tablets against vaginal estradiol. Both groups improved, with greater improvement on several outcomes in the estradiol group. It was not a trial of oral hyaluronic acid.

Other trials have studied vaginal gels, including a more recent pilot comparison with vaginal oestrogen. These findings support discussing a purpose-made vaginal moisturiser as an option; they do not establish that every product containing hyaluronic acid is equivalent. Choose a preparation intended for this use and follow its instructions.

A small study of an oral combination containing hyaluronic acid, glucosamine, lipoic acid and vitamins cannot establish that hyaluronic acid itself was responsible for improvement. Cosmetic skin benefits and vaginal benefits also need to be studied separately.

Sea buckthorn and fish oil are not established dryness treatments

One trial of sea buckthorn oil found a benefit in a measure of vaginal tissue integrity. Some other measures did not show a clear difference from placebo. That is a narrower finding than proving dependable relief from dryness for most people.

Fish oil is also marketed for vaginal comfort, but it does not have an established role as a replacement for recommended dryness treatments. Research about skin hydration or hormone levels cannot, by itself, demonstrate that a supplement improves vaginal symptoms.

Avoid interpreting an ingredient list as a treatment plan. Supplements can interact with medicines, and a natural label does not establish safety. Bring the exact products and doses to a pharmacist or clinician before combining them.

Sea buckthorn oil contains fatty acids, and fish oil supplies omega-3 fatty acids. Laboratory or skin-barrier findings about hydration, healing or collagen are not a substitute for reliable symptom trials in the vagina. Small studies in specific groups, including people treated for breast cancer, do not establish that high supplement doses are safe or effective for everyone.

DHEA is a hormone, not a vitamin

DHEA, also called prasterone, is converted in the body into other hormones. Prescription vaginal prasterone is used for selected menopause-related symptoms in some countries. It is different from an over-the-counter oral DHEA supplement.

The product, route and medical history determine whether it is suitable. Unexplained genital bleeding needs evaluation before treatment. If you have had breast cancer or are receiving hormone-blocking treatment, discuss options with your cancer-care team rather than assuming that DHEA is non-hormonal.

Increasing the amount of oestrogen in the bloodstream is not a goal to pursue with self-prescribed supplements. Oral DHEA should not be treated as interchangeable with a prescribed local vaginal preparation.

Start with options matched to your symptoms

A lubricant helps reduce friction during sexual activity. A vaginal moisturiser is used regularly to relieve ongoing dryness. They have different purposes, and some people use both. Avoid fragranced washes, douching and products that sting.

Use a condom-compatible lubricant if you use condoms; oil-based products can damage latex. Stop or change an activity that hurts rather than pushing through pain.

For menopause-related symptoms, a clinician may recommend low-dose vaginal oestrogen. It acts mainly locally and can sometimes be used alongside systemic HRT. Other prescription treatments are available when appropriate.

A history of breast cancer requires an individual discussion. Non-hormonal moisturisers and lubricants are usually considered first, and persistent symptoms can be reviewed with the relevant specialists. There are options beyond simply enduring the discomfort.

Judge progress by comfort and function

Keep a brief note of dryness, soreness, pain with sex and urinary symptoms, together with the products you try. Agree on a review if symptoms persist or treatment is uncomfortable.

The aim is lasting comfort with a suitable treatment, not a higher vitamin level or an expensive collection of supplements. If one approach does not help, the next step is to reconsider the cause and treatment together.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NICE recommends symptom-specific menopause care, including vaginal moisturisers, lubricants and local hormone options where appropriate, with individual discussion after breast cancer.

Trials of vaginal formulations cannot establish benefits of oral supplements. DHEA/prasterone is hormonal and should be distinguished from vitamins and non-hormonal moisturisers.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you compare the intended use and route of a product and prepare questions about dryness, painful sex and medical history. It cannot recommend a supplement dose for these symptoms.

When to seek help

Unexplained bleeding, persistent soreness or urinary symptoms should be assessed. Do not insert oral supplements or cosmetic oils into the vagina, and discuss hormonal products with a clinician.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • No vitamin is a proven universal remedy for vaginal dryness.
  • Oral supplements and purpose-made vaginal treatments are not interchangeable.
  • DHEA is hormonal and needs appropriate medical advice.
  • Lubricants, moisturisers and local prescription treatments have distinct roles.
  • Unexplained bleeding should be assessed rather than attributed to dryness.

Frequently asked questions

Can I put a vitamin capsule inside the vagina?

Do not use an oral supplement or cosmetic product this way. Vaginal preparations have specific formulations and instructions.

Will treating low vitamin D necessarily stop dryness?

No. Correcting a deficiency may benefit health, but dryness can have other causes and may need its own treatment.

Is vaginal hyaluronic acid the same as an oral beauty supplement?

No. Evidence for a vaginal moisturiser does not establish that a swallowed supplement will relieve vaginal symptoms.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
